subject: Parameters that are the bounded sum of other parameters

messages.author: abab84dd2ba42997
messages.subject: Parameters that are the bounded sum of other parameters
parts:
Hi Stan Users Group,

Apologies if this type of question has been covered directly elsewhere; I have looked through relevant posts here, here and here and also the manual under problematic posteriors. I've tried a few things but I'm still struggling to solve my problem.

I am trying to fit a three parameter nonlinear function to some data. I want to estimate how each of these parameters changes across a number of experimental conditions. To do this I thought to use a design matrix composed of sum-to-zero contrasts (created using Python equiv of r's contr.sum()). The beta weights of this design matrix are the offsets to the parameters caused by the conditions, and the intercept is the average parameter value across all the data. 

The problem comes in because the three parameters for the main model have bounds: specifically, all must be positive, and one also has an upper bound.

Example: parameter alpha is bounded between 0 and 5 (these constraints are determined by the problem setting). Here's a sketch of the relevant model components for alpha:

parameters {
  real<lower=0, upper=5> alpha;
  vector<lower=-5, upper=5>[D-1] alpha_offsets_raw;

...


transformed parameters {
    vector<lower=-3, upper=3>[D] alpha_offsets;
    # constrain offsets to sum to zero:
    for (i in 1:(D-1)) {
        alpha_offsets[i] <- alpha_offsets_raw[i];
    }
    alpha_offsets[D] <- -sum(alpha_offsets_raw);
...

model {
    alpha ~ normal(3, 1);
    alpha_offsets_raw ~ normal(0, 1);
   
    ...

    # loop over data rows:
    for (i in 1:N) {
        real this_alpha;
        this_alpha <- alpha + dot_product(X[i], alpha_offsets);
        ...
        y[i] ~ some_function(z[i], this_alpha, ...)
}

X is a design matrix (actually, N vectors of length D) of sum-to-zero (orthogonal) contrasts with the intercept column *removed* (because I add the intercept, alpha, manually). D is the number of coefficients in the design matrix and N are the observations (rows). 

In this model, this_alpha is not constrained to be between 0 and 5 even though alpha is. I would like this_alpha to also follow the constraint.

Some ideas:

  1. min / maxing the value of this_alpha to fall within 0 and 5 would achieve what I'm after, but won't play nice with gradients, as the manual warns.
  2. I thought maybe I could treat this_alpha as a linear predictor, passing it through the inv_logit function (multiplied by 5) to get a value bounded in the right range. I can see two problems with this: one, it adds an additional nonlinearity that makes the alpha and alpha_offsets parameters a bit hard to interpret and two, I'm not sure how to apply this to my other parameters (which have a lower bound of zero but no upper bounds – I suppose I could add some).
  3. Fitting all parameters on a log scale would solve the "must be positive" constraint, but again would require more gymnastics on parameter interpretation. Ideally I could have interpretable parameters on alpha and its offsets.
Any suggestions on a good way to parameterise this model would be much appreciated.

Thanks 

Tom

messages.author: abab84dd2ba42997
messages.subject: Re: Parameters that are the bounded sum of other parameters
parts:
Another way to think about this would be as a hierarchical model: each condition gets its own alpha parameter, which is drawn from a population alpha_mu and alpha_sigma. This could be used to create shrinkage between the alphas for each condition, and the difference scores between the samples would equate to the offsets (i.e. credible differences between conditions).

What I'm unsure about with that approach is that the next stage of this model will include effects for different people (i.e., I have a within-subjects / repeated measures design). That is, there would eventually be an alpha parameter for each [subject, condition]. In this case, I'm unsure how to build the hyperparameters to provide shrinkage both across conditions and across subjects.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Parameters that are the bounded sum of other parameters
parts:
The sum-to-zero constraint looks right, and I'm afraid the
only general way to proceed is your second suggestion, which
manually rescales the variables. That's because you have a
dependency on parameters.

The problem is how to use these parameters and a fixed (centered) data
matrix X:

> real<lower=0, upper=5> alpha;
> vector<lower=-5, upper=5>[D-1] alpha_offsets_raw;
to make sure this_alpha is in (0,5):

You can't really do it directly. One approach would be to
use a scaled inv_logit as you suggest:

this_alpha <- 5 * inv_logit(alpha + X[i] * alpha_offsets);

You can just declare X to be an array of row vectors or a matrix
and this product will work as written.

Given that you're not applying a prior directory to this_alpha,
you won't need a Jacobian correction for anything. It's just
like logistic regression, only you don't use this_alpha as
a parameter for a Bernoulli.

- Bob

messages.author: 71c315ee557ff234
messages.subject: Re: Parameters that are the bounded sum of other parameters
parts:
How about using a variant of the softmax function defined here:

http://de.mathworks.com/help/stats/multinomial-models-for-nominal-responses.html

You scale your variables by 5. K category is your sum. 

I think sum-to-zero constraints and limiting exclude themselves, eg. let all alpha -> max
then sum(alpha) cannot hold the limits.
